### Krystal Chan, DVM

#### Emergency

Dr. Chan grew up on the east coast. She received her Doctorate of Veterinary Medicine from Texas A&M University in 2018 and completed her internship in emergency and critical care medicine at DoveLewis Animal Emergency Hospital (Portland, Or) in 2019. She then went on to private practice as an emergency clinician in Houston, Tx. Her love of cooler weather brought her back to the Pacific Northwest. In her free time she enjoys snuggling with her cat (Kitten Little), traveling, scuba diving, and exploring vegetarian food options.

### Akiko Koshino, DVM DACVIM (Oncology)

#### Oncologist

Dr. Koshino grew up in Yokohama, Japan and received her veterinary degree from the University of Tokyo in 2005. It was during the clinical year at vet school that she developed a passion for oncology and after graduating, she moved to the Unites States to pursue further training. Following completion of a small animal rotating internship at Iowa State University, Dr. Koshino completed an oncology internship at Western Veterinary Specialist & Emergency Centre in Calgary, Canada. She then completed an oncology residency at Michigan State University and received board certification in medical oncology in 2015. After completing her residency, Dr. Koshino worked at private practices in Chicago for 5 years and has been working in the Seattle area since 2019.

Dr. Koshino offers a variety of treatments from advanced multimodal therapy to palliative care and believes that the patient’s quality of life is one of the most important factors in guiding treatment. She understands that a cancer diagnosis can be difficult and scary and is here to help the clients make the best decisions for their pets and family. Outside of work, she enjoys traveling, reading, and spending time with her husband and their daughter, two dogs, two cats, and tortoise.

## Oncology

Bellevue Veterinary Emergency + Specialty has Board Certified Oncologists on staff dedicated to the diagnosis, treatment, and management of cancer in pets.

# What does a Pet Oncologist do?

Veterinary oncologists work closely with pet owners and a multidisciplinary team to develop individualized treatment plans, which may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, and palliative care. By combining expertise in oncology and a deep understanding of animal behavior and physiology, veterinary oncologists strive to improve the quality of life and extend the precious time shared with beloved animal companions.

#### What to Expect

When visiting a veterinary oncologist, you can expect comprehensive and compassionate care for your pet facing a cancer diagnosis. The veterinary oncologist will conduct a thorough examination of your pet, review their medical history, and discuss any previous diagnostic tests or treatments. They will take the time to answer your questions and provide you with a clear understanding of the diagnosis, prognosis, and available treatment options.

The pet oncologist will work closely with you to develop a personalized treatment plan tailored to your pet’s specific needs, considering factors such as the type and stage of cancer, your pet’s overall health, and your preferences. Throughout the treatment journey, the veterinary oncologist will monitor your pet’s progress, adjust the treatment plan as necessary, and provide ongoing support and guidance. They are dedicated to maximizing your pet’s quality of life and supporting you and your family every step of the way.

Authors: Zierenberg Ripoll, Alexandra^{1}; Chin, Jessica^{1}; Schrempp, Diane^{1}; Kitchell, Barbara^{1}

^{1}VCA Veterinary Care Animal Hospital and Referral Center, Albuquerque, NM

Introduction: The aim of this study was to evaluate lomustine for treatment of Oral Malignant Melanoma (OMM).

Methods: Medical records of dogs treated with lomustine were evaluated for duration of response and toxicities. Data regarding treatment in a first-line vs. relapse-setting was extracted. Response was assessed visually as: CR (complete resolution of the lesion); PR (>50% regression of tumor); SD (<50 >25% growth of tumor). Duration of response was assessed as days from first treatment with lomustine until tumor progression. Survival was not assessed due to the use of additional treatment after lomustine failure.

Results: A total of 11 dogs were enrolled in the study. Eight dogs had pigmented OMM, 3 dogs had amelanotic melanoma. Lomustine was administered at a mean dose of 60 mg/m^{2} with a mean of 2 cycles of therapy administered at 21-day intervals. The entire cohort had 1 CR; 2 PR; 3 SD; and 5 PD. First-line therapy median duration of response was 48 days (range 27–92). Relapse-setting median duration of response was 41 days (range 18–99). Prior treatments included surgery, carboplatin and Oncept vaccine therapy. One dog required dose modification due to Grade II neutropenia. One Grade IV neutropenia was reported. Remaining toxicities included Grade I and Grade II diarrhea, vomiting, and lethargy. Median duration of response for the entire cohort was 42 days (range 18–99).

Conclusion: Lomustine chemotherapy provides modest benefit for dogs with OMM and minimal toxicity. As an oral therapy, lomustine is a cost-effective alternative for palliation of canine OMM.

Funding Information: No funding or conflicts of interest reported.
